```{python}
np.seterr(all="ignore")
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 80)
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)
pd.set_option("display.max_colwidth", 70)


def pct(x, decimals=2):
    return f"{100 * x:.{decimals}f}%"


def money(x, decimals=0):
    """Dollars for prose. Quarto escapes the dollar sign in inline output
    itself, so it must not be escaped here."""
    sign = "-" if x < 0 else ""
    return f"{sign}${abs(x):,.{decimals}f}"


def show_math(latex):
    """Print a display equation from a chunk marked `output: asis`."""
    print(f"$${latex}$$\n")


def tidy(obj, digits=4):
    """Round the numbers in a result for display, leaving text, whole
    numbers, and True/False alone."""
    def r(v):
        if isinstance(v, (bool, np.bool_)):
            return bool(v)
        if isinstance(v, (float, np.floating)):
            return int(v) if float(v).is_integer() and abs(v) >= 1 else round(float(v), digits)
        return v
    if isinstance(obj, pd.DataFrame):
        return obj.astype(object).apply(lambda col: col.map(r))
    return obj.astype(object).map(r)


def numbers(series, digits=4):
    """A result Series as a one-column table, without the prose fields."""
    keep = series.drop(labels=[k for k in ("conclusion",) if k in series])
    return tidy(keep, digits).to_frame("value")


def mnum(x, decimals=0):
    """A number with thousands separators that LaTeX will not mangle."""
    return f"{x:,.{decimals}f}".replace(",", "{,}")


faculty = pd.read_csv("data/big9_faculty_1999.csv")
agi = pd.read_csv("data/nevada_agi_2016_sample.csv")["AGI"].dropna()
MU_FAC = float(faculty["salary"].mean())
```

## Objectives

+ Distinguish a point estimate from an interval estimate, and say what the
  "95%" in a 95% confidence interval does and does not mean.
+ Build and interpret a confidence interval for a mean (with $t$, and with
  $z$ when $\sigma$ is known) and for a proportion.
+ Explain how the confidence level, the variability of the data, and the
  sample size each move the margin of error, and find the sample size a
  target margin requires.
+ State null and alternative hypotheses from a claim, before seeing the
  data, and choose between a one-tailed and a two-tailed test.
+ Define Type I and Type II errors as **false positives** and **false
  negatives**, with their probabilities $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
+ Calculate and correctly interpret a p-value for a $t$-test of a mean and a
  $z$-test of a proportion.
+ Use the link between a confidence interval and a two-tailed test.
+ Calculate and interpret the power of a test, and say how $\alpha$, the
  true effect, and $n$ change it.
+ Tell statistical significance from practical importance.

::: {.charcoal}
Chapter 7 asked: if we knew the population, how would a sample statistic
behave? These two chapters turn that question around. A manager holds *one*
sample and wants to say something about the population she cannot see. She
wants either a range for the unknown value ("average order size is between
\$118 and \$141") or a verdict on a claim ("the new kiosks really are faster
than five minutes").

Both answers come from one piece of machinery, built from the standard error
of Chapter 7:

$$\text{estimate}\ \pm\ (\text{critical value})\times(\text{standard error}).$$

Read as a range, it is a **confidence interval** (Chapter 8). Solved for
$n$, it tells you **how large a sample** to take (Chapter 8). Rearranged as
$(\text{estimate}-\text{claimed value})/\text{standard error}$, it is the
**test statistic** of a hypothesis test, and its tail area is the
**p-value** (Chapter 9). One engine, three uses. That is why we can cover
two chapters in one week, and it is the thread to hold on to.

As before, you will not compute these by hand on an exam. You will be handed
output, from Excel or from code, and asked what it means.
:::

# Part I: Confidence Intervals (Chapter 8)

## Point estimates and interval estimates

::: {.blue}
A **point estimate** is a single number computed from a sample to estimate a
population parameter: the sample mean $\bar{x}$ for $\mu$, the sample
proportion $\hat{p}$ for $p$.

An **interval estimate**, or **confidence interval**, is a range of values,
computed from the sample, constructed by a method that captures the
parameter in a stated share of samples, the **confidence level**, such as
95%.
:::

A point estimate is the best single guess, and it is almost certainly
wrong: Chapter 7 showed that $\bar{x}$ lands above or below $\mu$ by a
sampling error that changes from sample to sample. A point estimate says
nothing about how wrong it is likely to be. The interval does, and its
half-width has a name.

::: {.blue}
The **margin of error** is the distance from the point estimate to either end
of a confidence interval:

$$\text{margin of error}=(\text{critical value})\times(\text{standard error}),\qquad
\text{interval}=\text{estimate}\pm\text{margin of error}.$$
:::

## The three intervals of this week

| Parameter | Estimate | Standard error | Critical value | Excel margin of error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean, $\sigma$ known | $\bar{x}$ | $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ | $z_{\alpha/2}$ | `=CONFIDENCE.NORM(alpha, sigma, n)` |
| mean, $\sigma$ unknown (the usual case) | $\bar{x}$ | $s/\sqrt{n}$ | $t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ | `=CONFIDENCE.T(alpha, s, n)` |
| proportion | $\hat{p}=x/n$ | $\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}$ | $z_{\alpha/2}$ | `=NORM.S.INV(1-alpha/2)*SE` |

Here $\alpha=1-\text{confidence level}$, so a 95% interval has $\alpha=0.05$,
split as 0.025 in each tail. If the sample is more than 5% of a finite
population, multiply the standard error by the finite population correction
$\sqrt{(N-n)/(N-1)}$ exactly as in Chapter 7 (Section 8.6 of the text works
an example).

### When $\sigma$ is known

Your textbook starts here because the arithmetic is simplest. QVC samples 32
orders: $\bar{x}=\$129.20$, and the population standard deviation is taken
to be known, $\sigma=\$40.60$.

```{python}
#| label: qvc
qvc = interval_levels_table(129.2, 40.60, 32, levels=(0.90, 0.95, 0.99),
                            sigma_known=True)
qvc.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: qvc-stats
#| include: false
q95 = qvc.loc["95%"]
q90, q99 = qvc.loc["90%"], qvc.loc["99%"]
```

::: {.charcoal}
At 95%, we estimate that the average QVC order is between
`{python} money(q95["lower"], 2)` and `{python} money(q95["upper"], 2)`.
Asking for 99% confidence widens the interval to
`{python} money(q99["width"], 2)`, against `{python} money(q90["width"], 2)`
at 90%. **More confidence costs width.** The sample is the same in every
row; only the promise changed. (The textbook prints slightly different
limits because it rounds the standard error to 7.173 before multiplying.)
:::

In practice $\sigma$ is almost never known. If you knew the population's
standard deviation you would very likely know its mean too, and there would
be nothing to estimate. The realistic case replaces $\sigma$ with $s$, and
that changes the critical value.

## When $\sigma$ is unknown: the Student's $t$-distribution

::: {.blue}
When the sample standard deviation $s$ replaces $\sigma$, the standardized
mean

$$t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}$$

follows the **Student's $t$-distribution** with $n-1$ **degrees of freedom**
(df), provided the population is normal. The degrees of freedom count the
values free to vary once $\bar{x}$ is fixed: knowing the mean and $n-1$ of the
values pins down the last one.
:::

**Properties of the $t$-distribution**

+ Bell-shaped and symmetric around 0, with total area 1.
+ Flatter in the middle and **heavier in the tails** than the normal,
  because $s$ itself varies from sample to sample and adds uncertainty.
+ A family of curves, one for each df. As df grows, $s$ becomes a reliable
  stand-in for $\sigma$ and $t$ approaches the standard normal.
+ So the critical $t$ is always **larger** than the critical $z$ for the
  same confidence, and $t$-intervals are wider.

```{python}
#| label: t-curves
tx = np.linspace(-4.5, 4.5, 601)
_ = density_chart(tx, {"t, df = 3": t_pdf(tx, 3), "t, df = 10": t_pdf(tx, 10),
                       "t, df = 30": t_pdf(tx, 30),
                       "standard normal": normal_pdf(tx)},
                  title="The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal",
                  xlab="t or z")
```

```{python}
#| label: t-table
critical_value_table().round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: t-table-stats
#| include: false
t10, t30, t100 = (critical_value(0.95, df=d) for d in (10, 30, 100))
```

::: {.charcoal}
At 95% confidence the critical value is `{python} f"{t10:.3f}"` with 10 df,
`{python} f"{t30:.3f}"` with 30, and `{python} f"{t100:.3f}"` with 100,
against 1.960 for $z$. With small samples the difference matters; past a
hundred or so degrees of freedom it is cosmetic. Excel's
`=T.INV.2T(0.05, df)` returns these values.
:::

::: {.brown}
William Sealy Gosset worked out this distribution in 1908 while testing
barley and hops for the Guinness brewery in Dublin, where samples were small
and expensive. Guinness did not let its staff publish under their own names,
so he signed the paper "Student." The most-used small-sample method in
statistics came out of quality control in a business.
:::

### Application: Big Ten faculty salaries

In Chapter 7 we met the 215 economics faculty at Big Ten universities in
1999. Because we have the whole population, we know the true mean salary,
`{python} money(MU_FAC)`, and can check our interval against it. Pretend we
can afford to look at only 30 of them.

```{python}
#| label: fac-ci
fac_srs = simple_random_sample(faculty, 30, seed=21)["salary"]
fac_ci = mean_interval_from_data(fac_srs, 0.95)
numbers(fac_ci)
```

```{python}
#| label: fac-ci-math
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
show_math(rf"\bar{{x}}\pm t_{{0.025,\,29}}\frac{{s}}{{\sqrt{{n}}}}="
          rf"{mnum(fac_ci['estimate (x-bar)'])}\pm {fac_ci['critical value']:.3f}"
          rf"\times\frac{{{mnum(fac_ci['s (sample sd)'])}}}{{\sqrt{{30}}}}="
          rf"{mnum(fac_ci['estimate (x-bar)'])}\pm{mnum(fac_ci['margin of error'])}")
```

::: {.charcoal}
We estimate, with 95% confidence, that the mean salary of the 215 faculty is
between `{python} money(fac_ci["lower"])` and
`{python} money(fac_ci["upper"])`. The true mean,
`{python} money(MU_FAC)`, is
`{python} "inside" if fac_ci["lower"] <= MU_FAC <= fac_ci["upper"] else "outside"`
this interval. `{python} ("This particular sample ran " + ("high" if fac_ci["estimate (x-bar)"] > MU_FAC else "low") + ", by " + money(abs(fac_ci["estimate (x-bar)"] - MU_FAC)) + ", and the interval still reached the truth with " + money(min(MU_FAC - fac_ci["lower"], fac_ci["upper"] - MU_FAC)) + " to spare." if fac_ci["lower"] <= MU_FAC <= fac_ci["upper"] else "This particular sample missed. Nothing went wrong with the arithmetic.")`
Whether a given interval catches the truth is a matter of luck. How often
the method catches it is not, as the next section shows.
:::

::: {.brown}
The textbook's Dr. Gregg samples 18 patients and finds a mean of 100.3 with a
sample standard deviation of 16.6. Find the 95% confidence interval for the
population mean, and write the Excel formula for its margin of error. What
must be true of the population for this interval to be trustworthy with
only 18 observations?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{python}
#| label: gregg
gregg = mean_interval(100.3, 16.6, 18, 0.95)
numbers(gregg)
```

The interval is `{python} f"{gregg['lower']:.2f}"` to
`{python} f"{gregg['upper']:.2f}"`, with $t_{0.025,17}=$
`{python} f"{gregg['critical value']:.3f}"`. The margin of error is
`=CONFIDENCE.T(0.05, 16.6, 18)`. With $n=18$ the Central Limit Theorem
cannot be relied on, so the population itself must be close to normal.
:::

## What "95% confident" means

::: {.scarlet}
**A confidence interval is not a probability statement about $\mu$.** Once
the sample is drawn, the interval is fixed and so is $\mu$: the interval
either contains $\mu$ or it does not. There is nothing left to be random. It
is wrong to say "there is a 95% probability that $\mu$ is between
`{python} money(fac_ci["lower"])` and `{python} money(fac_ci["upper"])`."
:::

::: {.blue}
The **confidence level** describes the **method**, not any one interval: if
we drew sample after sample and built an interval from each in the same way,
95% of those intervals would capture $\mu$. The share that miss is $\alpha$.
"We are 95% confident" is shorthand for "this interval came from a method
that works 95% of the time."
:::

We can watch the method work, because for the faculty we know $\mu$. Each
horizontal line below is the 95% $t$-interval from a fresh sample of 30
(drawn with replacement, so the population behaves as if it were infinite).

```{python}
#| label: coverage-100
cov100 = simulate_intervals(faculty["salary"].to_numpy(), 30, MU_FAC,
                            level=0.95, reps=100, seed=8)
_ = interval_chart(cov100["lower"], cov100["upper"], MU_FAC,
                   estimates=cov100["x-bar"],
                   title="100 samples of 30 faculty, 100 confidence intervals",
                   xlab="Mean salary (dollars)")
```

```{python}
#| label: coverage-big
#| include: false
cov_fac = simulate_intervals(faculty["salary"].to_numpy(), 30, MU_FAC,
                             reps=100_000)["captured mu?"].mean()
cov_norm = simulate_intervals(lambda rng, shape: rng.normal(100, 16, shape),
                              30, 100, reps=100_000)["captured mu?"].mean()
hits100 = int(cov100["captured mu?"].sum())
```

::: {.charcoal}
`{python} hits100` of these 100 intervals captured the true mean, and
`{python} 100 - hits100` missed (in scarlet). Nothing about a miss looks
different from the inside: each was computed correctly from a perfectly good random
sample. You never learn which kind you are holding. That is the price of
estimating from a sample, and the confidence level is how you choose to pay
it.

Repeat the experiment 100,000 times and the share that capture the truth
settles down. From a normal population it is
`{python} pct(cov_norm, 1)`, as promised. From the faculty salaries it is
`{python} pct(cov_fac, 1)`, a little short of 95%, because salaries are
right-skewed and 30 observations do not fully cure that. Keep that number
in mind for the section after next.
:::

## The margin of error and its three levers

The margin of error is $(\text{critical value})\times s/\sqrt{n}$. Three
things move it, and a manager controls two of them.

1. **The confidence level.** Higher confidence means a larger critical value
   and a wider interval (the QVC table above).
2. **The variability of the data, $s$.** Noisier data, wider interval. You
   rarely control this, though a better measurement process or a stratified
   design (Chapter 7) can reduce it.
3. **The sample size, $n$.** Larger samples, narrower intervals, but through
   $\sqrt{n}$: to halve the margin you need about **four times** the data.

```{python}
#| label: me-sizes
me_n = interval_sizes_table(29_500, [25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 1_600])
me_n.round({"standard error": 1, "critical value": 3, "margin of error": 1})
```

```{python}
#| label: me-sizes-stats
#| include: false
me100, me400 = me_n.loc[100, "margin of error"], me_n.loc[400, "margin of error"]
```

::: {.charcoal}
With a standard deviation like the faculty salaries' (about \$29,500), a
sample of 100 gives a 95% margin of error of `{python} money(me100)`;
quadrupling to 400 gives `{python} money(me400)`, a little better than half
because the critical $t$ also falls. Precision is expensive. The next
section turns this around and asks how large a sample a target margin
requires.
:::

## When is the $t$-interval trustworthy?

::: {.blue}
The $t$-interval assumes the **population is normal**. The assumption
matters most when $n$ is small. As $n$ grows, the Central Limit Theorem makes
$\bar{x}$ close to normal anyway, and the $t$-procedure becomes reliable for
most populations, **but how large is "large" depends on how skewed the
population is.**
:::

The textbook's rule of thumb is $n\ge30$. The honest version is a
simulation. Below, we draw thousands of samples from a population whose mean
we know, compute the $t$-statistic for each, and compare its distribution
with the $t$-curve it is supposed to follow. On the left the population is
normal. On the right it is the Nevada adjusted gross income file from
Chapter 7, which is strongly right-skewed.

```{python}
#| label: t-sim-charts
#| layout-ncol: 2
mu_agi = float(agi.mean())
t_norm = simulate_t_statistics(lambda rng, shape: rng.normal(0, 1, shape), 10, 0)
t_agi = simulate_t_statistics(agi.to_numpy(), 10, mu_agi)
grid = np.linspace(-5, 5, 401)
_ = density_histogram(t_norm[np.abs(t_norm) < 5], grid, t_pdf(grid, 9),
                      bins=60, title="Normal population, n = 10",
                      xlab="t statistic", curve_label="t, df = 9")
_ = density_histogram(t_agi[np.abs(t_agi) < 5], grid, t_pdf(grid, 9),
                      bins=60, title="Nevada AGI (skewed), n = 10",
                      xlab="t statistic", curve_label="t, df = 9")
```

The pictures hint at the problem; the tail counts measure it. These are the
actual error rates of 5% one-tailed tests, which is the same as asking how
often a one-sided 95% bound would miss.

```{python}
#| label: t-sim-rates
rates = {}
for name, pop, mu in (("normal", lambda rng, shape: rng.normal(0, 1, shape), 0.0),
                      ("Nevada AGI", agi.to_numpy(), mu_agi)):
    for n in (10, 30, 100, 400):
        if name == "normal" and n > 30:
            continue
        rates[f"{name}, n = {n}"] = t_tail_rates(
            simulate_t_statistics(pop, n, mu), n)
tail_rates = pd.DataFrame(rates).T
tail_rates.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| label: t-sim-stats
#| include: false
agi30 = tail_rates.loc["Nevada AGI, n = 30"]
agi400 = tail_rates.loc["Nevada AGI, n = 400"]
```

::: {.charcoal}
With a normal population the $t$-procedure does exactly what it promises,
even at $n=10$. With the skewed income data at $n=30$, a test that is
supposed to be wrong 5% of the time in the lower tail is wrong
`{python} pct(agi30["lower-tailed test rejects"], 1)` of the time, and in
the upper tail only `{python} pct(agi30["upper-tailed test rejects"], 1)`.
The errors pile up on one side. Even at $n=400$ the two tails are
`{python} pct(agi400["lower-tailed test rejects"], 1)` and
`{python} pct(agi400["upper-tailed test rejects"], 1)`. Two-tailed
procedures fare better, because the two errors partly cancel.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**"$n\ge30$" is a starting point, not a guarantee.** For incomes, sales,
claims, wait times and anything else with a long right tail, look at the
data before trusting a $t$-interval or $t$-test, and be most careful with
one-tailed tests. Your textbook suggests that a larger sample helps "where
the $t$-distribution can be approximated by the normal distribution." The
reason a larger sample helps is the Central Limit Theorem acting on
$\bar{x}$, not $t$ turning into $z$. Chapter 12 introduces a formal check of
normality.
:::

## A confidence interval for a proportion

::: {.blue}
For a population proportion, with $x$ successes in a sample of $n$ and
$\hat{p}=x/n$,

$$\hat{p}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} .$$

The normal approximation needs enough successes and failures:
$n\hat{p}\ge5$ and $n(1-\hat{p})\ge5$ (many texts ask for 10; the stricter
rule is safer).
:::

The textbook surveys 175 people, of whom 116 have the characteristic of
interest, and asks for a 99% interval.

```{python}
#| label: prop-ci
pci = proportion_interval(116, 175, 0.99)
numbers(pci)
```

::: {.charcoal}
The sample proportion is `{python} f"{pci['estimate (p-hat)']:.3f}"`, and
with 99% confidence the population proportion is between
`{python} f"{pci['lower']:.3f}"` and `{python} f"{pci['upper']:.3f}"`, a
margin of error of `{python} f"{pci['margin of error']:.3f}"`, or about
`{python} f"{100 * pci['margin of error']:.0f}"` percentage points. News
reports of polls quote this margin, almost always at 95%.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
The standard error here uses $\hat{p}$, because the interval makes no claim
about $p$ and $\hat{p}$ is the best we have. When we *test* a claimed
proportion in Part II, the standard error will use the claimed value
instead. Students mix these up more than anything else in the proportion
material.
:::

## How large a sample do you need?

This is the most practical result in Chapter 8. Set the margin of error you
can live with, $E$, and solve for $n$.

::: {.blue}
**For a mean:** $n=\left(\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma}{E}\right)^2$.

**For a proportion:** $n=\dfrac{z_{\alpha/2}^2\,p(1-p)}{E^2}$.

**Always round up.** Rounding down gives a margin slightly larger than you
asked for. $\sigma$ and $p$ are *planning values* from a pilot study or past
data. With no information about $p$, use $p=0.5$, which makes $p(1-p)$ as
large as it can be, so the sample is never too small.
:::

```{python}
#| label: n-examples
pd.DataFrame({
    "AT&T: mean, sigma = 400, E = 75, 95%": tidy(sample_size_mean(400, 75, 0.95), 3),
    "proportion, p = 0.12, E = 0.05, 98%": tidy(sample_size_proportion(0.05, 0.98, 0.12), 3),
    "proportion, p = 0.5, E = 0.05, 98%": tidy(sample_size_proportion(0.05, 0.98, 0.5), 3),
}).T.fillna("")
```

```{python}
#| label: n-stats
#| include: false
n_att = sample_size_mean(400, 75)
n12 = sample_size_proportion(0.05, 0.98, 0.12)
n50 = sample_size_proportion(0.05, 0.98, 0.5)
```

::: {.charcoal}
AT&T needs `{python} f"{n_att['n (round UP)']:.0f}"` customers: the formula
gives `{python} f"{n_att['(z sigma / E)^2']:.2f}"`, and 109 would fall just
short. For the proportion, a prior estimate of 12% requires
`{python} f"{n12['n (round UP)']:.0f}"`; with no prior information
(p = 0.5) it takes `{python} f"{n50['n (round UP)']:.0f}"`. Knowing
something about $p$ in advance saves more than half the sample.

The textbook reports 230 and 543. It uses $z=2.33$ from its table; Excel's
`=NORM.S.INV(0.99)` gives 2.326, and the extra precision moves each answer by
one. Either is acceptable. Just be consistent.
:::

```{python}
#| label: n-halving
sample_size_table([0.08, 0.04, 0.02, 0.01], level=0.95, p=0.5)
```

::: {.charcoal}
**Halving the margin of error quadruples the sample.** This one table
explains why national polls settle on about 1,000 respondents (a margin
near three points) and almost never pay for the 10,000 that would buy one
point.
:::

::: {.brown}
A Las Vegas resort wants to estimate the average amount a convention
attendee spends on property, to within \$15 with 95% confidence. Last year's
survey suggests a standard deviation of about \$110. **(a)** How many
attendees should it survey? **(b)** It also wants the share who would return
next year, to within 4 points at 95%, with no prior estimate. How many for
that? **(c)** One survey will ask both questions. How many responses does it
need?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{python}
#| label: resort-n
r_mean = sample_size_mean(110, 15, 0.95)
r_prop = sample_size_proportion(0.04, 0.95, 0.5)
pd.DataFrame({"(a) mean": tidy(r_mean, 3),
              "(b) proportion": tidy(r_prop, 3)}).T.fillna("")
```

**(a)** `{python} f"{r_mean['n (round UP)']:.0f}"`. **(b)**
`{python} f"{r_prop['n (round UP)']:.0f}"`. **(c)** The larger of the two,
`{python} f"{max(r_mean['n (round UP)'], r_prop['n (round UP)']):.0f}"`, so
that both targets are met. And in practice more than that, since not
everyone asked will answer, a nonsampling problem (Chapter 7) that no
formula fixes.
:::

# Part II: Hypothesis Testing (Chapter 9)

## The logic of a test

::: {.blue}
A **hypothesis** is a claim about a population parameter, such as a mean or
a proportion.

The **null hypothesis**, $H_0$, is the status quo or the claim being
tested. It always contains the equality: $=$, $\le$, or $\ge$ a specific
value.

The **alternative hypothesis**, $H_1$, is what we would conclude if the data
are strong enough evidence against $H_0$. It never contains the equality:
$\ne$, $<$, or $>$.
:::

A hypothesis test is a trial. $H_0$ is the defendant, presumed innocent. The
data are the evidence. The verdict is **reject $H_0$** (guilty: the evidence
is strong enough) or **do not reject $H_0$** (not guilty: it is not). A jury
never declares a defendant *innocent*, only *not guilty*, because a lack of
evidence is not proof of innocence.

::: {.scarlet}
**We never "accept" $H_0$.** Failing to reject it means the data are
**consistent with** $H_0$, not that they show it is true. The same data are
usually consistent with many other values too. Your textbook occasionally
says a sample "supports the original assumption" after a failure to reject.
Read that as "fails to contradict."
:::

## Stating the hypotheses

Three claims, three setups.

::: {.charcoal}
**Time on a web page.** A study reported in the *Wall Street Journal*
([Does the Internet Make You Smarter?](https://crooker.faculty.unlv.edu/mba775/articles/Does_the_Internet_Make_You_Smarter_-WSJ-2010-06-03.pdf)
and
[Does the Internet Make You Dumber?](https://crooker.faculty.unlv.edu/mba775/articles/Does_the_Internet_Make_You_Dumber_-WSJ-2010-06-04.pdf))
says the average American looks at a web page for 56 seconds. A student
wants to know whether UNLV students are *different*, in either direction:

$$H_0:\mu=56\qquad H_1:\mu\ne56\qquad\text{(two-tailed)}$$

**Light bulb life.** A lab wants evidence that a new bulb *lasts longer*
than the industry's 8,000 hours. The claim needing evidence goes in $H_1$:

$$H_0:\mu\le8{,}000\qquad H_1:\mu>8{,}000\qquad\text{(one-tailed, upper)}$$

**An 18-game NFL season.** The commissioner says a majority of fans favor
it. The players' union, which opposes it, wants evidence that the
commissioner is wrong:

$$H_0:p\ge0.5\qquad H_1:p<0.5\qquad\text{(one-tailed, lower)}$$
:::

::: {.blue}
A **two-tailed test** has $H_1:\ne$ and looks for a difference in either
direction. A **one-tailed test** has $H_1:<$ or $H_1:>$ and looks in one
direction only.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Choose the hypotheses and the tail before you look at the data.** $H_1$ is
the claim that *requires evidence*, not the answer you are hoping for. A
one-tailed p-value is half the two-tailed one, so choosing the tail after
seeing which way the data point turns a two-tailed p of 0.08 into a
one-tailed 0.04 and an "insignificant" result into a "significant" one. That
is not analysis; it is a thumb on the scale. When in doubt, test two-sided.
:::

## Two ways to be wrong: false positives and false negatives

Because the verdict rests on a sample, it can be wrong in two ways, and the
two mistakes have very different costs.

In the language of testing, a **positive** result is a test that **rejects
$H_0$**: it reports that it found something, an effect, a difference, a
disease, a fraud, a benefit. A **negative** result is a test that does
**not** reject $H_0$: it reports that it found nothing.

::: {.blue}
A **Type I error** is a **false positive**: rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is
actually true. The test reports an effect that is not there. Its probability
is $\alpha$, the **significance level**, which we choose:

$$\alpha=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ is true}).$$

A **Type II error** is a **false negative**: failing to reject $H_0$ when
$H_0$ is actually false. The test misses an effect that is there. Its
probability is $\beta$:

$$\beta=P(\text{do not reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ is false}).$$

The **power** of a test is the probability of a **true positive**,
correctly rejecting a false $H_0$: $\text{power}=1-\beta$.
:::

```{python}
#| label: error-table
error_table()
```

| | $H_0$ actually true (nothing there) | $H_0$ actually false (something there) |
|---|---|---|
| **Courtroom** ($H_0$: innocent) | convict an innocent person: **false positive, Type I** | acquit a guilty person: **false negative, Type II** |
| **Smoke alarm** ($H_0$: no fire) | alarm sounds, no fire: **false positive, Type I** | fire, no alarm: **false negative, Type II** |
| **Spam filter** ($H_0$: real mail) | real mail sent to spam: **false positive, Type I** | spam reaches the inbox: **false negative, Type II** |
| **Audit** ($H_0$: no fraud) | honest account flagged: **false positive, Type I** | fraud goes undetected: **false negative, Type II** |

::: {.charcoal}
A memory aid: a Type I error is **crying wolf** (an alarm with no wolf); a
Type II error is **missing the wolf**. "Positive" never means "good"; it
means the test said *yes, something is here*. A positive cancer screen is
bad news and a positive drug trial is good news; a *false* positive is a
wrong "yes" either way.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**Your textbook gets these labels backwards in one place.** The Focus on
Analytics box on the FDA's drug approvals, at the end of Section 9.5, says
"a Type I error (false negative)" and "a Type II error (false positive)." It
is the other way around. With $H_0$: *the drug has no benefit*,

+ approving a drug that does not work is rejecting a true $H_0$: a **Type I
  error, a false positive**;
+ refusing a drug that does work is failing to reject a false $H_0$: a
  **Type II error, a false negative**.

The box's own definitions and its decision figure are correct; only the two
parenthetical labels are swapped. Use the definitions above on exams.
:::

::: {.charcoal}
The FDA example is still worth reading for its point about costs. A false
positive (a harmful or useless drug approved) produces identifiable victims
and headlines, so regulators guard hard against it with a small $\alpha$. A
false negative (a beneficial drug refused) produces victims nobody can
name, people who would have been helped, so it gets less attention. A
small $\alpha$ buys protection against the visible error at the price of a
larger $\beta$, more of the invisible one. Which error is worse is a
business or policy judgment, not a statistical one, and it should drive the
choice of $\alpha$.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
$\alpha$ is $P(\text{reject}\mid H_0\text{ true})$, the false positive rate
*among situations where nothing is there*. It is **not** the probability that
a rejection is a false positive, $P(H_0\text{ true}\mid\text{reject})$. That
second number also depends on how often $H_0$ is true to begin with: the
base-rate problem of the screening-test example in Chapter 4. If a company
tests 100 marketing ideas and only a few really work, a good share of its
"significant" results will be false positives even at $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

In quality control, a Type I error (rejecting a good batch) is sometimes
called the **producer's risk** and a Type II error (accepting a bad batch)
the **consumer's risk**. The structure is the same.

$\alpha$ and $\beta$ pull against each other. For a fixed sample size,
making it harder to cry wolf makes it easier to miss the wolf. The only way
to reduce both at once is a larger sample. We return to this with numbers
at the end of the chapter.

## The p-value

::: {.blue}
The **p-value** is the probability, **computed assuming $H_0$ is true**, of
getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, in the
direction(s) of $H_1$.

**Decision rule:** reject $H_0$ if $p\le\alpha$; otherwise do not reject.
:::

A small p-value says: *if* $H_0$ were true, data like ours would be rare.
Either we saw something rare, or $H_0$ is false. Below $\alpha$, we bet on
the second. This is the same reasoning we used to judge the commute claim in
Chapter 7. The p-value is simply that tail probability, given a name.

::: {.scarlet}
**What the p-value is not.**

+ It is **not** the probability that $H_0$ is true. It is computed by
  *assuming* $H_0$ is true, so it cannot also measure whether it is.
+ It is **not** "the confidence you have that your null hypothesis is
  correct," as your textbook says in Section 9.2. A p-value of 0.30 does not
  mean we are 30% sure of $H_0$.
+ It is **not** the size or importance of an effect. A tiny, worthless effect
  can have a tiny p-value if the sample is big enough (see the end of this
  note).
:::

Your textbook adds that a p-value "can be computed directly only for $z$."
That was a limit of printed tables, not of the method. Excel's `T.DIST`,
`T.DIST.RT`, and `T.DIST.2T` give exact $t$ p-values, and the book itself uses
them in Section 9.3.

## The six steps

1. State $H_0$ and $H_1$ (before seeing the data).
2. Choose $\alpha$, by weighing the cost of a false positive against a false
   negative.
3. Identify the test statistic and its distribution under $H_0$ (and, if you
   use them, the critical values).
4. Compute the test statistic from the sample.
5. Compute the p-value and compare it with $\alpha$ (equivalently, compare
   the statistic with the critical value).
6. State the conclusion **in the words of the problem**, including the
   direction, and never "accept $H_0$."

For a mean with $\sigma$ unknown, the test statistic is

$$t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}},\qquad\text{df}=n-1,$$

where $\mu_0$ is the value **claimed in $H_0$**. The numerator is not
$\bar{x}-\mu$: we do not know $\mu$, and the whole calculation asks how far
$\bar{x}$ is from what $H_0$ says.

## Application: a one-tailed $t$-test

Target pilots self-service checkout kiosks. A cashier checkout averages 5
minutes, and Target will adopt the kiosks only if they are faster. Twelve
kiosk checkouts average $\bar{x}=4.2$ minutes with $s=1.42$. Test at
$\alpha=0.05$.

$$H_0:\mu\ge5\qquad H_1:\mu<5$$

```{python}
#| label: target
target = t_test(4.2, 1.42, 12, 5, "less", 0.05)
numbers(target)
```

```{python}
#| label: target-chart
c_t = critical_value(alpha=0.05, tails=1, df=11)
_ = test_chart(grid, t_pdf(grid, 11), target["test statistic t"],
               critical=-c_t, alternative="less",
               p_value=target["p-value"],
               title="Kiosks: the t-distribution with 11 df, if H0 is true",
               xlab="t")
```

::: {.charcoal}
$t=$ `{python} f"{target['test statistic t']:.2f}"`, and the p-value is
`{python} f"{target['p-value']:.4f}"` (Excel:
`{python} target["Excel p-value"]`). If kiosks really took 5 minutes or
more on average, a sample of 12 averaging 4.2 or less would turn up only
about `{python} pct(target["p-value"], 1)` of the time. That is below
$\alpha=0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: **the data are evidence that average
kiosk checkout time is less than 5 minutes.** The statistic is also past the
critical value, `{python} f"{-c_t:.3f}"`; the two comparisons always agree.

Two cautions before Target rips out the registers. With $n=12$ the test
relies on checkout times being roughly normal, and checkout times are
usually right-skewed, exactly the case where a one-tailed test misbehaves
(the simulation above). And "less than 5 minutes" could mean 4.9: the next
step is a confidence interval for how much faster.
:::

## Application: a two-tailed $t$-test

Nielsen says the average American watches 34.5 hours of television a week.
Ten people average $\bar{x}=39.6$ hours with $s=16.4$. Is the claim wrong,
in either direction? Use $\alpha=0.02$.

$$H_0:\mu=34.5\qquad H_1:\mu\ne34.5$$

```{python}
#| label: nielsen
nielsen = t_test(39.6, 16.4, 10, 34.5, "two-sided", 0.02)
numbers(nielsen)
```

```{python}
#| label: nielsen-chart
c_n = critical_value(alpha=0.02, tails=2, df=9)
_ = test_chart(grid, t_pdf(grid, 9), nielsen["test statistic t"],
               critical=c_n, alternative="two-sided",
               p_value=nielsen["p-value"],
               title="Nielsen: both tails count in a two-tailed test",
               xlab="t")
```

::: {.charcoal}
$t=$ `{python} f"{nielsen['test statistic t']:.2f}"`. In a two-tailed test,
a result as far *below* 34.5 would be just as much evidence against $H_0$,
so the p-value counts both tails:
`{python} f"{nielsen['p-value']:.3f}"` (Excel:
`{python} nielsen["Excel p-value"]`, which needs the *absolute value* of
$t$). That is far above 0.02, so we do not reject $H_0$: **the sample is
not evidence that Americans' average viewing differs from 34.5 hours.**

It is *not* evidence that the average **is** 34.5. Ten people with a
standard deviation of 16 hours could hardly contradict any claim within
several hours of 39.6. The next section makes "several hours" precise.
:::

## Tests and confidence intervals are the same calculation

::: {.blue}
A two-tailed test at significance level $\alpha$ rejects $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$
**exactly when** $\mu_0$ lies outside the $(1-\alpha)$ confidence interval.
The confidence interval is the set of all claimed values the test would not
reject.
:::

```{python}
#| label: duality
nielsen_ci = mean_interval(39.6, 16.4, 10, 0.98)
print(f"98% interval: {nielsen_ci['lower']:.2f} to {nielsen_ci['upper']:.2f}\n")
interval_test_agreement(39.6, 16.4, 10, [20, 25, 34.5, 50, 55], alpha=0.02).round(4)
```

::: {.charcoal}
The 98% interval runs from `{python} f"{nielsen_ci['lower']:.1f}"` to
`{python} f"{nielsen_ci['upper']:.1f}"` hours. Any claim in that range
survives a two-tailed test at $\alpha=0.02$; any claim outside it is
rejected. Notice how wide that is: the same ten people "fail to reject"
25 hours and 50 hours. That is why failing to reject 34.5 says so little.

This is the most useful fact in these two chapters. **The interval tells you
everything the two-tailed test does, and more**: not only whether the claim
survives, but which other values would. When you report a test, report the
interval too. (Your textbook does this with an iPhone price claim of \$811:
the 95% interval $797.8\pm1.96(5.41)$ excludes 811, so the claim is
rejected.)
:::

::: {.scarlet}
The match is exact only for a **two-tailed** test with
$\text{confidence}=1-\alpha$. A one-tailed test at $\alpha=0.05$ matches a
one-sided 95% bound, or equivalently a two-sided **90%** interval.
:::

## Application: light bulbs, with the truth known

The old version of this note simulated a light-bulb study so that we would
know the right answer. A new bulb's life in hours is normal with mean 8,050
and standard deviation 225, so it *does* last longer than 8,000, and $H_0$
is false. The lab tests 100 bulbs.

```{python}
#| label: bulbs
bulb_rng = np.random.default_rng(20261026)
bulbs = bulb_rng.normal(8_050, 225, 100)
bulb = t_test_from_data(bulbs, 8_000, "greater", 0.05)
numbers(bulb)
```

```{python}
#| label: bulbs-stats
#| include: false
bulb_rej = bool(bulb["reject H0?"])
bulb_power = simulate_rejections(
    lambda rng, shape: rng.normal(8_050, 225, shape), 100, 8_000,
    "greater", 0.05)["rejection rate"]
```

::: {.charcoal}
The sample averages `{python} f"{bulb['x-bar']:,.1f}"` hours, $t=$
`{python} f"{bulb['test statistic t']:.2f}"`, p-value
`{python} f"{bulb['p-value']:.4f}"`.
`{python} ("We reject H0, the correct decision, since we built the population so that the bulbs really do last longer." if bulb_rej else "We do not reject H0, and that is the WRONG decision: we built the population so that the bulbs really do last longer. This is a Type II error, a false negative, caught in the act. Nothing was done incorrectly. The sample simply came in low, and 100 bulbs were not enough to be sure of detecting a 50-hour improvement.")`

How often would this study find the improvement? Run it 20,000 times on
fresh samples: it rejects $H_0$ `{python} pct(bulb_power, 1)` of the time.
That is the study's **power**. About `{python} pct(1 - bulb_power, 0)` of
the time, a perfectly good study of a genuinely better bulb would report
"no evidence of improvement."
:::

## Testing a proportion

::: {.blue}
To test $H_0:p=p_0$ (or $\le$, $\ge$), with $\hat{p}=x/n$,

$$z=\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} ,$$

valid when $np_0\ge5$ and $n(1-p_0)\ge5$. The p-value comes from the
standard normal.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
**The standard error uses $p_0$, the value claimed in $H_0$, not $\hat{p}$.**
The test asks how surprising $\hat{p}$ would be *if $H_0$ were true*, so it
uses the spread that $H_0$ implies. The confidence interval, which claims
nothing, uses $\hat{p}$.
:::

### Application: women on French corporate boards

France required large companies to move toward 40% women on their boards.
In 2017, 34% of board members were women. Has the share risen? A sample of
240 board members finds 96 women. Test at $\alpha=0.05$.

$$H_0:p\le0.34\qquad H_1:p>0.34$$

```{python}
#| label: france
france = proportion_test(96, 240, 0.34, "greater", 0.05)
numbers(france)
```

```{python}
#| label: france-chart
zx = np.linspace(-4, 4, 401)
_ = test_chart(zx, normal_pdf(zx), france["test statistic z"],
               critical=critical_value(alpha=0.05, tails=1),
               alternative="greater", p_value=france["p-value"],
               title="French boards: standard normal, if H0 is true", xlab="z")
```

```{python}
#| label: france-se
#| include: false
se_test = sqrt(0.34 * 0.66 / 240)
se_ci = sqrt(0.40 * 0.60 / 240)
```

::: {.charcoal}
$\hat{p}=$ `{python} f"{france['p-hat']:.2f}"`, $z=$
`{python} f"{france['test statistic z']:.2f}"`, and the p-value is
`{python} f"{france['p-value']:.4f}"`. Below 0.05, so we reject $H_0$: **the
data are evidence that the share of women on large French boards has risen
above 34%.** The standard error was `{python} f"{se_test:.4f}"`, computed
from $p_0=0.34$; using $\hat{p}=0.40$ would have given
`{python} f"{se_ci:.4f}"`, a different (and wrong) $z$.
:::

::: {.brown}
**Finishing the NFL example.** Suppose the players' union polls 400 randomly
chosen fans and 186 favor an 18-game season. (These numbers are
illustrative.) **(a)** State $H_0$ and $H_1$. **(b)** Test at $\alpha=0.05$
and state the conclusion in words. **(c)** Find a 95% confidence interval for
the share of fans in favor. Which standard error did you use in (b), and
which in (c)?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{python}
#| label: nfl
nfl = proportion_test(186, 400, 0.5, "less", 0.05)
nfl_ci = proportion_interval(186, 400, 0.95)
numbers(nfl)
```

**(a)** $H_0:p\ge0.5$ (the commissioner's claim), $H_1:p<0.5$ (what the
union wants evidence for). **(b)** $\hat{p}=$
`{python} f"{nfl['p-hat']:.3f}"`, $z=$
`{python} f"{nfl['test statistic z']:.2f}"`, p-value
`{python} f"{nfl['p-value']:.4f}"`.
`{python} ("Reject H0: the poll is evidence that fewer than half of fans favor the change." if nfl["reject H0?"] else "Do not reject H0: although fewer than half of this sample favor the change, the poll is not strong enough evidence that fewer than half of ALL fans do.")`
**(c)** `{python} f"{nfl_ci['lower']:.3f}"` to
`{python} f"{nfl_ci['upper']:.3f}"`. The test used $p_0=0.5$ in its
standard error; the interval used $\hat{p}=$ `{python} f"{nfl['p-hat']:.3f}"`.
:::

## When $\sigma$ is known: the $z$-test

When the population standard deviation is known, the test statistic is
$z=(\bar{x}-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})$ and the p-value comes from the standard
normal. Everything else is identical. Your textbook works several examples
this way in Section 9.2; read them for the steps, and use the $t$-test in
practice.

```{python}
#| label: cfl
cfl = z_test(8_120, 500, 36, 8_000, "greater", 0.05)
numbers(cfl)
```

::: {.charcoal}
The textbook's Edalight example: 36 new compact fluorescent bulbs average
8,120 hours, and $\sigma=500$ hours is taken as known. Testing
$H_0:\mu\le8{,}000$ against $H_1:\mu>8{,}000$ gives $z=$
`{python} f"{cfl['test statistic z']:.2f}"` and p-value
`{python} f"{cfl['p-value']:.4f}"`, which is above $\alpha=0.05$: not
enough evidence that the new bulb lasts longer than 8,000 hours.
:::

::: {.scarlet}
Excel's `Z.TEST(range, mu0, sigma)` returns the **upper-tail** p-value only.
For a lower-tailed test use `1 - Z.TEST(...)`; for a two-tailed test,
`2 * MIN(Z.TEST(...), 1 - Z.TEST(...))`. (The textbook's description of its
arguments calls $\sigma$ "the population mean"; it is the population
standard deviation.)
:::

## Type II errors and power

$\alpha$ is chosen. $\beta$ is not: it depends on how wrong $H_0$ actually
is, on $\alpha$, and on $n$. To compute it we must pick a specific "true"
value, because "$H_0$ is false" covers infinitely many possibilities.

### Application: the Nissan Leaf battery

Nissan's Leaf averages 151 miles per charge. A new battery is claimed to do
better. Nissan will test 50 cars, with $\sigma=12$ miles known and
$\alpha=0.05$:

$$H_0:\mu\le151\qquad H_1:\mu>151 .$$

::: {.blue}
The **critical sample mean** $\bar{x}_\alpha$ is the value of $\bar{x}$ at the
edge of the rejection region. For an upper-tailed test,

$$\bar{x}_\alpha=\mu_0+z_\alpha\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} ,$$

(with $-$ for a lower-tailed test). If the true mean is $\mu_1$,

$$\beta=P\!\left(\bar{x}<\bar{x}_\alpha\ \middle|\ \mu=\mu_1\right),
\qquad\text{power}=1-\beta .$$
:::

```{python}
#| label: leaf
leaf = power_mean(151, 12, 50, 156, 0.05, "greater")
numbers(leaf)
```

```{python}
#| label: leaf-chart
leaf_cut = critical_mean(151, 12, 50, 0.05, "greater")
_ = power_chart(151, 156, 12 / sqrt(50), leaf_cut, "greater",
                title="Nissan Leaf: alpha, beta, and power on one picture",
                xlab="Average range of 50 cars (miles), x-bar")
```

::: {.charcoal}
Nissan rejects $H_0$ if the 50 cars average more than
`{python} f"{leaf_cut:.2f}"` miles. If $H_0$ is true (top panel), that
happens 5% of the time: the false positive rate. Now suppose the new
battery really averages 156 miles (bottom panel). The test misses it
whenever the sample mean falls short of `{python} f"{leaf_cut:.2f}"`, which
happens with probability $\beta=$
`{python} f"{leaf['beta = P(Type II error)']:.4f}"`. The power, the chance
of correctly detecting the better battery, is
`{python} f"{leaf['power = 1 - beta']:.4f}"`.

(The textbook gets 0.0968 and 0.9032 by rounding $z$ to $-1.30$. Its
version of the calculation is correct.)
:::

We can check $\beta$ the same way we checked the confidence level: test
many fresh samples from a world where the mean really is 156, and count.

```{python}
#| label: leaf-sim
leaf_sim = simulate_rejections(lambda rng, shape: rng.normal(156, 12, shape),
                               50, 151, "greater", 0.05, sigma=12)
numbers(leaf_sim)
```

::: {.charcoal}
The simulated studies fail to reject `{python} pct(leaf_sim["failed to reject (rate)"], 2)`
of the time, against the formula's
`{python} pct(leaf["beta = P(Type II error)"], 2)`. The formula is not
magic; it is a shortcut to what would happen if we ran the study over and
over.
:::

### Power depends on how big the real effect is

```{python}
#| label: leaf-curve
leaf_pt = power_table(151, 12, 50, np.arange(151, 160.5, 0.5))
_ = line_chart(leaf_pt.index, {"power": leaf_pt["power"]},
               title="Power curve: the chance of detecting the better battery",
               xlab="True average range (miles)", ylab="Power = 1 - beta",
               hlines=[0.05, 0.80], ylim=(0, 1.02))
leaf_pt.loc[[151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156, 157, 158]].round(4)
```

::: {.charcoal}
If the true mean is barely above 151, the test almost never notices: power
starts at $\alpha=0.05$ (at exactly 151, rejecting *is* a Type I error) and
is only `{python} pct(leaf_pt.loc[152, "power"], 0)` at 152 miles. Power
passes 80% somewhere between 155 and 156. **A test can see large effects
easily and small ones hardly at all.** Before trusting a "no significant
difference," ask how large a difference the study could have detected.

(The textbook's Table 9.10 shows 0.0495 at 151, which should be exactly
0.05; it comes from rounding $z_\alpha$ to 1.65.)
:::

### Power depends on $\alpha$

```{python}
#| label: leaf-alpha
ab = alpha_beta_table(151, 12, 50, 157, alphas=(0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025,
                                                0.05, 0.10, 0.20))
ab_curve = alpha_beta_table(151, 12, 50, 157, alphas=np.linspace(0.001, 0.20, 60))
_ = line_chart(ab_curve.index, {"beta (false negative)": ab_curve["beta"]},
               title="Lowering alpha raises beta (n = 50, true mean 157)",
               xlab="alpha (false positive rate)", ylab="beta",
               vlines=[0.01, 0.05, 0.10], markers=False)
ab.round(4)
```

::: {.charcoal}
At a true mean of 157 miles, cutting $\alpha$ from 0.05 to 0.01 raises
$\beta$ from `{python} f"{ab.loc[0.05, 'beta']:.4f}"` to
`{python} f"{ab.loc[0.01, 'beta']:.4f}"`. Fewer false positives, more
false negatives: there is no free lunch.

The textbook reports $\beta=0.1190$ for this case. It rounds $z_{0.01}$ to
2.33 and then rounds the critical mean to 155 miles before computing
$\beta$; unrounded, the critical mean is
`{python} f"{critical_mean(151, 12, 50, 0.01):.2f}"` and
$\beta=$ `{python} f"{ab.loc[0.01, 'beta']:.4f}"`. The lesson is the same,
but if you work in Excel you will match this note, not the book.
:::

### Power depends on the sample size, which you control

The textbook says the only way to reduce both errors at once is a larger
sample. Here is how much larger. Suppose the improvement worth detecting is
3 miles (true mean 154):

```{python}
#| label: leaf-n
leaf_n = power_by_n(151, 12, [10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200], 154)
need = n_for_power(151, 12, 154, power=0.80)
leaf_n.round(4)
```

::: {.charcoal}
With 50 cars, Nissan would detect a 3-mile improvement only
`{python} pct(leaf_n.loc[50, "power"], 0)` of the time, close to a coin
flip. To reach the conventional 80% power it needs
`{python} f"{need['n (round UP)']:.0f}"` cars, from

$$n=\left(\frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)\,\sigma}{\mu_1-\mu_0}\right)^2
=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.842)\times12}{3}\right)^2 .$$

This is the calculation to do **before** a study, alongside the
margin-of-error calculation of Chapter 8. A study too small to detect the
effect that matters is a study designed to say "no evidence," and it will
usually oblige.
:::

::: {.brown}
Explore this yourself in the interactive app below. Change the true mean,
the hypothesized mean, $\sigma$, and $n$, and watch $\alpha$, $\beta$, and
the power move.

<a href="https://jcrooker.shinyapps.io/statistical-inference-mean/"
   target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
   style="background-color:#A03123; color:white; padding:12px 20px;
          text-decoration:none; border-radius:6px; font-weight:bold;">
   Launch the interactive simulation
</a>
:::

::: {.brown}
Buick owners have averaged 59 years old. After an advertising campaign aimed
at younger buyers, Buick will survey 41 new owners and test
$H_0:\mu\ge59$ against $H_1:\mu<59$ at $\alpha=0.10$, with $\sigma=10$
years. **(a)** Find the critical sample mean. **(b)** If the campaign really
lowered the average age to 58, what is the power? **(c)** Is this a
well-designed study? How many owners would give 80% power against a true
mean of 58?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

```{python}
#| label: buick
buick = power_mean(59, 10, 41, 58, 0.10, "less")
buick_n = n_for_power(59, 10, 58, 0.80, 0.10, "less")
numbers(buick)
```

**(a)** `{python} f"{critical_mean(59, 10, 41, 0.10, 'less'):.2f}"` years: Buick
rejects $H_0$ if the sample averages less than that. **(b)**
`{python} f"{buick['power = 1 - beta']:.4f}"`. **(c)** No. Even at
$\alpha=0.10$, the survey would detect a one-year drop only about
`{python} pct(buick['power = 1 - beta'], 0)` of the time. Reaching 80% power
takes `{python} f"{buick_n['n (round UP)']:,.0f}"` owners. Either survey far
more people or decide in advance that a one-year change is too small to
matter.
:::

## Statistically significant is not the same as important

::: {.blue}
A result is **statistically significant** when $p\le\alpha$: the data are
unlikely under $H_0$. It is **practically significant** when the effect is
large enough to matter for the decision. The first is a statistical
question; the second is a business one.
:::

```{python}
#| label: practical
big_n = t_test(4.95, 1.42, 20_000, 5, "less", 0.05)
big_ci = mean_interval(4.95, 1.42, 20_000, 0.95)
pd.Series({"x-bar (minutes)": f"{4.95:.2f}", "n": f"{20_000:,}",
           "p-value": f"{big_n['p-value']:.7f}",
           "95% interval: lower": f"{big_ci['lower']:.3f}",
           "95% interval: upper": f"{big_ci['upper']:.3f}"}).to_frame("Target, all stores")
```

::: {.charcoal}
Suppose Target rolls the kiosks out and logs 20,000 checkouts averaging 4.95
minutes. The p-value is about
`{python} f"{big_n['p-value']:.7f}"`, overwhelming evidence that kiosks are
faster than 5 minutes. By about **three seconds**. That is statistically
significant and commercially irrelevant. The confidence interval shows it
at once, which is another reason to report one.

The opposite also happens: a small study of an important effect, like the
41-owner Buick survey, can easily come back "not significant." **Large
samples find trivial effects; small samples miss important ones.** Always
ask *how big* as well as *whether*.
:::

# Reading the Textbook: Corrections

Donnelly is a clear guide to the mechanics, and the reading for these
chapters is assigned. A few statements in it will cost you points if you
copy them:

::: {.scarlet}
1. **False positive / false negative (Section 9.5, Focus on Analytics).**
   The labels are reversed. A Type I error is a **false positive**; a Type
   II error is a **false negative**.
2. **"The p-value can also be described as the confidence you have that
   your null hypothesis is correct" (Section 9.2).** No. It is computed
   assuming $H_0$ is true and says nothing directly about the probability
   that $H_0$ is true.
3. **"The sample supports the original assumption."** After a failure to
   reject, the data are *consistent with* or *fail to contradict* $H_0$.
   They do not support it.
4. **"p-values can be computed directly only for $z$."** Only from the
   printed table. Excel's `T.DIST` family gives exact $t$ p-values.
5. **Larger $n$ helps "where the $t$-distribution can be approximated by the
   normal."** Larger $n$ helps because the Central Limit Theorem makes
   $\bar{x}$ more normal. For skewed populations $n=30$ may not be enough.
6. **Rounding.** `NORM.S.INV(0.95)` returns 1.645, not 1.654 as printed.
   The book's rounded $z$-values (2.33, 1.65) move some sample sizes by one
   and some $\beta$ values in the second decimal place. Match Excel, and say
   so.
:::

# Which Procedure Is It?

::: {.brown}
For each, name the procedure (interval or test; mean with $z$ or $t$, or
proportion), write $H_0$ and $H_1$ where there is a test, and say whether
it is one- or two-tailed.

**(a)** A casino host samples 45 high-limit players' average session length
to estimate the mean for all such players.

**(b)** A hotel claims at least 90% of guests rate their stay 4 stars or
better. A consumer group samples 300 reviews and wants evidence that the
claim overstates satisfaction.

**(c)** A packaging line is supposed to fill 18-ounce boxes. Quality control
samples 25 boxes an hour and wants to catch under-filling *or*
over-filling.

**(d)** A marketing director wants to estimate the share of app users who
would pay for a premium tier to within 3 points.

**(e)** A new call-routing system is adopted only if it cuts average hold
time below the current 4.5 minutes. Twenty calls are sampled.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Solution

| | Procedure | Hypotheses | Tails |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | $t$-interval for a mean | none | (two-sided interval) |
| (b) | $z$-test for a proportion, SE from $p_0=0.90$ | $H_0:p\ge0.90$, $H_1:p<0.90$ | one (lower) |
| (c) | $t$-test for a mean | $H_0:\mu=18$, $H_1:\mu\ne18$ | two |
| (d) | sample size for a proportion, then a $z$-interval | none | (two-sided interval) |
| (e) | $t$-test for a mean (check skewness: $n=20$ and hold times are skewed) | $H_0:\mu\ge4.5$, $H_1:\mu<4.5$ | one (lower) |

In (d), with no prior estimate use $p=0.5$:
`{python} f"{sample_size_proportion(0.03, 0.95)['n (round UP)']:,.0f}"`
users at 95% confidence.
:::

### Your own junior analyst

The lab script answers the questions in this note. The skill to practice is
getting a *new* question answered and checking the answer:

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> A Las Vegas restaurant group says its average ticket is \$62. I sampled 40
> tickets last weekend: the mean was \$67.40 and the standard deviation was
> \$21.30. By running code, (1) give me a 95% confidence interval for the
> average ticket, (2) test whether the average differs from \$62 at
> alpha = 0.05 and give the exact p-value, and (3) tell me whether the two
> answers agree and why they must. Then state, in one sentence each, what a
> Type I error and a Type II error would mean here, and label each as a false
> positive or a false negative. Finally, tell me whether n = 40 is large
> enough to trust a t-procedure for restaurant tickets, and how you would
> check.
:::

Check four things in the reply: the $t$ critical value has 39 degrees of
freedom; the p-value is two-tailed; the Type I error is labelled a **false
positive** (concluding the average differs when it does not); and the
answer to the last question is not simply "yes, because 40 is more than 30."

### Working in Excel

::: {.prompt}
Prompt

> Build me an Excel workbook that shows what "95% confidence" means. Sheet 1
> has input cells for a true mean (100), a true standard deviation (16), a
> sample size n (30), and a confidence level (0.95). Sheet 2 draws 100
> samples of size n with =NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd), and for each computes
> x-bar, s, the margin of error with CONFIDENCE.T, the lower and upper
> limits, and a column that says TRUE if the interval contains the true mean.
> Report the share of TRUE at the top, and chart the 100 intervals as
> horizontal error bars against a vertical line at the true mean. Give me the
> file to download.
:::

Press F9 a dozen times and note the share each time. Then change the
confidence level to 0.80 and repeat. In one paragraph: what changed, what
did not, and what does that tell you about the meaning of the word
"confidence"?
